title: Building better prediction models for consumer choices
excerpt: As consumers, we are constantly making choices about things like what to eat at a restaurant, what clothing to buy at a store and the type of car we'd like to purchase, and so much more. Savvy producers of such goods look to economists to help estimate what products people want and how demand might shift when factors like price and availability change.
content_html:
As consumers, we are constantly making choices about things like what to eat at a restaurant, what clothing to buy at a store and the type of car we'd like to purchase, and so much more. Savvy producers of such goods look to economists to help estimate what products people want and how demand might shift when factors like price and availability change.

For many years, economists have relied on something called the random utility model (RUM)—a fundamental framework for rational decision-making widely used in empirical analysis in economics, marketing and many other fields—to help predict consumer decision-making. However, there are problems with using the model when the full variety of options is unknown.

This issue is related to the linear ordering problem and is one that has remained unsolved since researchers across applied mathematics and mathematical psychology first started exploring it in the 1980s. Now, researchers led by Kota Saito, professor of economics at Caltech, and MIT graduate student Alec Sandroni (BS '25), have solved one of the main challenges that arises when RUM is used with incomplete data sets.

"Our findings may help improve predictions of individual choice when all the options are not observable," explains Saito, who is co-author of a paper published in the August issue of the American Economic Review about the team's work.

RUM is the foundation of a method called discrete choice analysis, which economists use to model consumer decisions statistically to help inform pricing strategies, antitrust analysis, policy evaluation across industries and more. It describes how a group of consumers with diverse preferences makes choices, but only when all options are clearly defined. When all possible choices aren't defined, economists often group the alternatives into an "outside option."

"We found that even if you don't observe which outside alternative gets chosen, you can get a surprising amount of information just by looking at what wasn't chosen. Some of this information might get ignored in the typical methods," says Sandroni, who worked with Saito throughout his undergraduate career as a Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowships (SURF) program student.

In fact, Sandroni, Saito and Haruki Kono, a graduate student at MIT and a third collaborator on the study, found that the outside-option tool can produce severely biased estimates. Using network flow theory—a computational method often used to model the movement of entities such as traffic and fluids—the researchers were able to clarify the limitation of the outside-option approach.

"Using our innovation, you can test for RUM with less data than we thought necessary for the RUM to work well," Sandroni says. "People can use our new technique to better evaluate the demand in a variety of industries."

Sandroni, who was a mathematics major at Caltech, is continuing to work with Saito to investigate additional challenges in analyzing consumer choice, but he hasn't always been interested in economics.

"I thought I was going to do environmental science or physics when I first came to Caltech," he says. "But then I was looking for SURFs, I found a little math test that Kota has on his website. I think I was the only one who solved it that year, so we started working together, and I'm still studying economics today."

Although Sandroni knew little about the topic before starting the research project, Saito says he worked at a very high level on the recently published paper, generating ideas, completing rigorous proofs and finalizing the manuscript.

"Alec quickly learned what he needed to do, and the fact that he could walk with me throughout the years is really impressive," Saito says. "The requirements of the work were very demanding for an undergraduate student, but he overcame these difficulties."

Yuexin Liao (BS '26), who is now a graduate student in mathematics and computer science at Caltech, investigated another decision-making query related to RUM last summer for a SURF project with Saito and Sandroni. In economic studies where an individual selects one option from a finite set of mutually exclusive alternatives, many data sets group choices into broad labels—for example, a car model with many trims, or the single "outside option." The main question of the project is: "When does this kind of aggregation faithfully reflect how people actually choose?"

The team showed that aggregation creates an ambiguity of composition, meaning that the grouped label may hide different underlying options for different people or markets. Under this ambiguity, the RUM has surprisingly weak testable implications. A recent working paper by the group was the first to formally study the implications of this ambiguity in the composition of aggregated alternatives. The paper was accepted by two well-recognized international conferences in economic theory; Sandroni presented the paper this summer, which is unusual as a first-year graduate student.

Saito has now recruited a new SURF student, Vivian Loh, a rising third-year student in mathematics. Loh, Saito and Sandroni have initiated new challenges, including a proposal for a model that can describe human choice more generally through simple conditions called monotonicity. They also aim to apply economic decision theory to machine learning.

"I enjoy working with undergraduates because they are often open to very difficult questions and bring new approaches to the problems," Saito says.

Publication details

Haruki Kono et al, Random Utility with Unobservable Alternatives, American Economic Review (2026). DOI: 10.1257/aer.20240712

content_html_zh:
作为消费者，我们不断地做出选择，比如在餐馆吃什么、在商店买什么衣服以及我们想要购买的汽车类型等等。 精明的此类商品生产商希望经济学家帮助估计人们想要什么产品，以及当价格和供应等因素发生变化时，需求可能会如何变化。

多年来，经济学家一直依靠随机效用模型（RUM）——广泛应用于经济学、营销和许多其他领域的实证分析中的理性决策的基本框架——来帮助预测消费者决策。 然而，当选项的全部种类未知时，使用该模型会出现问题。

这个问题与线性排序问题相关，自从应用数学和数学心理学的研究人员在 20 世纪 80 年代首次开始探索以来，这个问题一直悬而未决。 现在，由加州理工学院经济学教授 Kota Saito 和麻省理工学院研究生 Alec Sandroni (BS '25) 领导的研究人员已经解决了 RUM 与不完整数据集一起使用时出现的主要挑战之一。

Saito 解释说：“当所有选项都不可观察时，我们的发现可能有助于改善对个人选择的预测。”Saito 是《美国经济评论》八月号上发表的一篇关于该团队工作的论文的合著者。

RUM 是离散选择分析方法的基础，经济学家用这种方法对消费者决策进行统计建模，以帮助为定价策略、反垄断分析、跨行业政策评估等提供信息。 它描述了一群具有不同偏好的消费者如何做出选择，但前提是所有选项都被明确定义。 当所有可能的选择都没有被定义时，经济学家经常将替代方案归为“外部选项”。

“我们发现，即使你不观察选择了哪种外部替代方案，你也可以通过查看未选择的内容来获得数量惊人的信息。 其中一些信息在典型方法中可能会被忽略。”Sandroni 说，他作为夏季本科生研究奖学金 (SURF) 项目的学生在整个本科生涯中与 Saito 一起工作。

事实上，桑德罗尼、齐藤和麻省理工学院的研究生、该研究的第三位合作者河野春树发现，外部选择工具可能会产生严重偏差的估计。 利用网络流理论（一种通常用于模拟交通和流体等实体运动的计算方法），研究人员能够澄清外部选择方法的局限性。

“利用我们的创新技术，您可以使用比我们认为 RUM 正常运行所需的数据更少的数据来测试 RUM，”Sandroni 说。 “人们可以使用我们的新技术更好地评估各个行业的需求。”

桑德罗尼是加州理工学院数学专业的学生，​​他正在继续与斋藤合作，研究分析消费者选择方面的其他挑战，但他并不总是对经济学感兴趣。

“当我第一次来到加州理工学院时，我以为我会学习环境科学或物理学，”他说。 “但后来我在寻找 SURF，我在 Kota 的网站上发现了一个小数学测试。 我想那一年我是唯一解决这个问题的人，所以我们开始一起工作，而我今天仍在学习经济学。”

尽管桑德罗尼在开始研究项目之前对这个主题知之甚少，但齐藤说，他在最近发表的论文中以非常高的水平工作，产生想法，完成严格的证明并最终确定手稿。

“亚历克很快就知道了他需要做什么，而且他能和我一起走过这些年，这真的令人印象深刻，”斋藤说。 “工作的要求对于一个本科生来说非常苛刻，但他克服了这些困难。”

Yuexin Liao（BS '26）现在是加州理工学院数学和计算机科学专业的研究生，去年夏天与 Saito 和 Sandroni 一起在 SURF 项目中调查了另一个与 RUM 相关的决策查询。 在经济研究中，个人从一组有限的相互排斥的替代方案中选择一个选项，许多数据集将选择分为广泛的标签，例如，具有多种装饰的汽车模型，或单个“外部选项”。 该项目的主要问题是：“这种聚合何时才能忠实反映人们的实际选择？”

该团队表明，聚合会造成成分的模糊性，这意味着分组标签可能会隐藏针对不同人群或市场的不同潜在选项。 在这种模棱两可的情况下，RUM 的可测试含义出人意料地微弱。 该小组最近发表的一份工作文件首次正式研究了这种模糊性对综合替代方案构成的影响。 该论文被两个公认的经济理论国际会议接受；桑德罗尼今年夏天发表了这篇论文，这对于一年级研究生来说是不寻常的。

Saito 现在招收了一名新的 SURF 学生 Vivian Loh，她是一名正在崛起的数学专业三年级学生。 Loh、Saito 和 Sandroni 提出了新的挑战，包括提出一种模型的建议，该模型可以通过称为单调性的简单条件更普遍地描述人类的选择。 他们还旨在将经济决策理论应用于机器学习。

“我喜欢与本科生一起工作，因为他们经常对非常困难的问题持开放态度，并提出解决问题的新方法，”斋藤说。
